abstract: An arXiv preprint by Tuhin Chakrabarty, Xinyue Liu, Jane C. Ginsburg and Paramveer Dhillon applying full-text AI detection to 14,419 self-published genre-fiction books sold on Amazon between 2023 and 2026, matched to daily sales records through June 2026. The paper tests the common assumption that AI-generated books are low-quality output that buyers ignore, and finds instead that they reach commercial scale and take an increasing share of top-rank sales positions. Its central claim is structural rather than qualitative: generative AI reshapes a creative market by flooding it with supply, diluting per-title revenue for everyone, and displacing human-authored work from the scarce discovery slots that drive sales.
keyFindings: "Over this period, the number of books with observed sales in a quarter grew 19.2-fold, while quarterly revenue grew only 8.9-fold. The market therefore added selling books faster than it added revenue, and revenue per selling book fell across most genres."

Books with detected AI text above 25 percent "make up a large share of the catalog but a smaller share of sales," yet still "reach commercial scale, winning a growing share of sales over time and taking more of the scarce top-rank positions once held by books with no detected AI text."
"Books with no AI text lose the most ground in genres with high AI diffusion, and most of all where Kindle Unlimited availability is high."

Among top-selling books, those with substantial AI text "draw on more distinctive language from existing books than do books with no AI text; for these books overlap rises with revenue, a gradient we do not detect for books with no AI text."
"None of these books disclose whether or not they contain AI-produced content," so the dilution operates without any signal available to buyers.
"Generative AI can thus reshape a creative market through scale rather than quality."
methodology: Full-text AI detection applied to 14,419 self-published genre-fiction titles sold on Amazon from 2023 to 2026, with a threshold of greater than 25 percent detected AI text defining the substantial-AI category. Titles are matched to daily sales records running through June 2026, permitting quarterly aggregation of both selling-title counts and revenue. Comparisons are made across genres stratified by AI diffusion and by Kindle Unlimited availability. A separate analysis measures distinctive-language overlap with pre-existing books among top sellers.
qualifiers: This is an unreviewed arXiv preprint filed under computer science categories (cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.CY) rather than economics, though the corpus tiers comparable working papers at Tier 1. It is plotted as an overlay rather than a data point because its outcome variables map to no graph construct: the creative industry displacement graph is denominated in percent of roles displaced, and this paper measures market revenue dilution with no worker denominator at all. The freelancer rate graph was considered and rejected because the roughly 54 percent implied fall in revenue per selling title is arithmetically driven by the 19.2-fold catalog expansion, making it a composition effect rather than a decline in any individual author's realised rate; no conversion in the proxy metric methodology supports treating it otherwise. Scope is self-published genre fiction on a single retail platform, which is a narrow and unusually AI-permeable slice of creative work and should not be generalised to commissioned or traditionally published creative labour. Detection of AI text is probabilistic and the 25 percent threshold is a modelling choice.
